results.title: Sexual harassment
results.description: Covers unwelcome physical contact, a demand or request for sexual favours, showing pornography without consent, and making sexually coloured remarks.

results.title: Voyeurism
results.description: Watching or capturing the image of a woman doing a private act where she expects privacy, or distributing such an image, even if she had consented only to the image being captured and not shared.

results.title: Stalking
results.description: Repeatedly following or contacting a woman despite her clear disinterest, or monitoring her internet, email, or electronic communication. Courts have confirmed this covers purely online conduct such as repeated messages on WhatsApp or social media.

results.title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman
results.description: Covers a word, sound, gesture, or object intended to insult a woman's modesty, including where it intrudes on her privacy — this can extend to online comments and messages.

results.title: Dowry death
results.description: Applies when a woman dies from burns, bodily injury, or in otherwise unusual circumstances within 7 years of marriage, and there is evidence of cruelty or harassment for dowry shortly before her death.

results.title: Cruelty by husband or his relatives
results.description: Makes it an offence for a husband or his relatives to subject a married woman to cruelty. Read together with Section 86, which defines what counts as cruelty.

results.title: "Cruelty" defined
results.description: Defines cruelty as wilful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury, or harassment aimed at coercing her (or her family) to meet an unlawful demand such as dowry.

results.title: Extortion
results.description: Intentionally putting someone in fear of injury to induce them to hand over money, property, or a signed document — this includes threatening to publish something damaging (such as an image) unless paid.

results.title: Cheating
results.description: Dishonestly inducing a person to deliver property, or to do or omit something they otherwise would not, by deception. Graded by severity; the most serious form still carries up to 7 years' imprisonment.

results.title: Cheating by personation
results.description: Cheating by pretending to be someone else — including a real or entirely invented person — such as impersonating a bank official, a relative, or a fake profile used to defraud someone.

results.title: Criminal intimidation
results.description: Threatening someone with injury to their person, reputation, or property to cause alarm or force them to act (or not act). Threats made anonymously, or to falsely accuse someone of a serious crime, carry higher punishment.

results.title: Defamation
results.description: Making or publishing a false statement about someone that harms their reputation, whether spoken, written, or posted online. BNS adds community service as an alternate punishment.

results.title: Registration of FIR, Zero FIR, and e-FIR
results.description: Any police station must register an FIR for a cognisable offence regardless of where it happened ("Zero FIR"), and now also recognises electronic filing ("e-FIR") — the informant must sign it within 3 days. For sexual offences, a woman's statement must be recorded by a woman police officer, and the process must be videographed.

results.title: Escalating to the SP if police refuse to register an FIR
results.description: If a police station refuses to register your FIR for a cognisable offence, you can send a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police, who can direct that it be registered and investigated.

results.title: Applying to a Magistrate to order an investigation
results.description: If the police and the SP both fail to act, you can approach a Magistrate directly (usually after showing you tried the police route first) to order that the police investigate.

results.title: Penalty for damage to a computer or computer system
results.description: Civil liability (compensation) for unauthorised access, downloading, or damaging data, introducing viruses, or denying access to a computer resource without the owner's permission.

results.title: Identity theft
results.description: Fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's password, digital signature, or other unique identification feature — carries up to 3 years' imprisonment and a fine.

results.title: Cheating by personation using a computer resource
results.description: Cheating someone by pretending to be another person through a computer resource or communication device — e.g. a fake profile, cloned account, or spoofed message used to defraud someone.

results.title: Violation of privacy
results.description: Intentionally capturing, publishing, or transmitting an image of a person's private area without consent, in circumstances violating their privacy.

results.title: Publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically
results.description: Covers publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form — first conviction up to 3 years' imprisonment, rising for repeat offences.

results.title: Publishing or transmitting sexually explicit material electronically
results.description: A more serious offence than Section 67, covering material containing a sexually explicit act — carries higher punishment, up to 5 years on first conviction.

results.title: Breach of confidentiality and privacy
results.description: Applies when someone who obtained access to personal data under a contract or official duty (e.g. a platform employee, service provider) discloses it without consent.
